THE LATE BUILDERS' STRIKE.

Now that the fight between the carpenters
and joiners, and master builders has been
brought to a close, it may be of use to go over
the battle-field, count the cost, and critioise
the tactics of the contending parties.

_
• Of the employers little need be said, little
can be said, as what they did was, as a rule,
done covertly, and without anyone being the
wiser as to whether they blundered or net.
At the commencement they made a very
serious mistake in demanding the right to
nominate the arbitrators. They rectified this,
however, without much loss of time, and it is
only necessary to note it now as an indication
of the arbitrary and high-handed way in
which they have been in the habit of dealing
with the people in their employment.
_

To our readers the conduct of the men is of
far more importance, and, therefore, of much
greater interest. Their mode of conducting
and concluding this strike is connected with
the welfare of the great labour cause, and
every man who takes an interest in that cause,
now that the conflict is over, should try to
understand whether the men who led in this
contest fought their battle in a way creditable
to themselves and profitable to the cause on be-
half of which they took the field. Of the 9
hours, the 9d., and the working code of rules
whoih constituted the men's original de m and, wo
say nothing, holding that sellers of labour
have a right to the conditions of sale to
their own commodity. We shall not, there-
fore, canvass the reasonableness or unreason-
ableness of what the mon asked for, especially
as we consider that this did not to any groat
extent decide the issue of the struggle; it is
the manner' in which the contest was carried
on we are interested in, and to that we
shall chiefly draw our readers' attention.
In the first place, we ask whether any-
thing can, justify a struggle deliberately
entered on by a body of skilled artizans
without the necessary trades union organiza-
tion ? If we .are rightly informed, the great
bulk of the men on strike were not in union,
did not, in fact, belong to the union exist-
ing in their own trade. They took the field as
an undisciplined, dissatisfied crowd, without
organization, without tried leaders, without
resources—not as a society provided with the
necessaries of war. They must have been
absolutely blind to the teachings of the last
half-century to believe for one moment that
they were not placing themselves at a fatal
disadvantage by stri)Ling whilst in such a eon-
dition, especially as their trade was not enjoy-
ing; like so many other branches of industry,

an exceptional prosperity. To lose in a con-
flict thus entered on was almost a certainty.
The thought of winning under such circum-
stances was an old stupid fallacy a thousand
times exploded, and yet these carpenters and
joiners, men of the metropolis, with a union
in their own trade readymade to their hands,
with its doors open. to receive them, with a
treasured experience to guide them, preferred
to trust their fortunes to a struggle, from
which discipline, order, authority in command,
and all else that gives force to a movement
were almost necessarily absent. If the battles
of labour can be won under circumstances of
this sort, trades unions are mistakes—costly
and troublesome blunders which ought to be
avoided.

The effect of this on the fortunes of the fight
aro unmistakeable, as may be seen by the
following paragraph taken from the 'Daily
News of August 23rd :—" The .most of the
closed shops in the published list of the car-
penters and joiners are at no loss for labour,
if not completely full. fn fact, the shops with
empty benches were clearly indicated, and
these were pronounced, for the most part, to '
be 'union shops '—that is, shops where the
employes have hitherto been society men."
This circumstance tells its own tale, and if
anything can point out to non-society MOD
the value of union they ought to see it by the
spirit of loyalty and pluck here displayed by
men who have got in them the confidence that
discipline and resources give.
Another point which should not be over-
looked is the different position men ooeupy
who go into action relying on their own funds,
from that occupied by those who cannot take
a step unless supported by the funds of others.
It is a folly for any body of working men to
remain without the resources organization
gives. It is a humiliation to solicit aid from
the charity or generosity of others. What
right has any body.of men, after .neglecting
the duty of providing funds for themselves, to
ask support from those who have been more
thoughtful and provident? Surely the men
who, at the end of a long struggle, were glad to
accept a compromise which might have been
made at first without the loss of a week's
work, will take a lesson from this, and at
once,. in a spirit of manliness and good sense,
join themselves to their brothers in union,
who, in the heat of the struggle, 'stood most
firmly to their colours, and who, when the
retreat became inevitable, held the enemy in
cheek, and. forced conditions of peace which
the broken, disorderly mob of routed non-
unionists could never have secured for them-
selves.

Again, what could be more fatuitous than
the conduct of the men in cutting off their old
leaders, because employers and men in their
interest had fixed upon them the name of" agi-
tators." Mr. SADLER and those who acted
with him said they desired to show their em-
ployers that they could successfully conduct
their trades affairs without the aid of such
men. They have not proved this, but some-
thing which most people will regard as quite
the contrary. This was not a blunder only,
it was a crime. It is telling men not of their
own order, but of their own trade even, that
the more efficient the service they give, the
less tit they are to help them, and the more
deserving of reproaoh,aud ingratitude. It is
giving_ the world practical ass in twee that ex-
pe,rienee is of no use, and that the better a
man understands anything the less fit he is to

deal with it. This wretched blunder has,
however, been severely punished, and we
hope, even for tha sake of the men who sug-
gested and upheld so preposterous a doctrine,
that we shall hear no more of it, as even
the experience they have gained in fighting
a losing battle, if utilized in a sensible and
modest way, may give their service a value
in the future which can scarcely be claimed
for it in the work which has just passed from
their hands.

The grossest blunder of aU, however, was
the rejection of arbitration. Working men
are to blame for rejecting this when fairly
Offered under
.any pretence whatever. The
most hopeful position does not warrant it, but
when men entering on a contest almost wholly
unprepared reject it, Or travestie it by the
conditions they seek to attach to it, such a
proceeding can scarcely be regarded otherwise
thanes an insanity. The first thought Connected'
with any matter in dispute is that arbitration
removes it from settlement by force to settle-
ment by reason in a spirit of equity. The
past evil treatment of working men by their
employers has been the result of force, always
conspioionsly on the side of capital. It is true.
that more perfect Union amongst the men is
redressing the balance, is equalizing this force.
Still as working men only seek for equitable
adjustments, their policy is to encourage
methods of settlement most favourable to the
just: claims of all concerned. The right to
strike Must not be given up, and the duty of
preparing for such a disagreeable contingency'
should not be neglected. These must not be
brought into question. But the prime and
principal obligation resting on working men is
to settle their disputes by friendly agreement
' with their employers, without serious inter-
ference with the comfort of their families,
or without unnecessary interruption of the
business in which they are engaged. If we
look at this strike we shall see that what has
been obtained, nay more, might have been got
the first week by a quiet and sensible arbi-
tration. Indeed, much that has been conceded
by the men might, we think, have been
retained had they been of themselves as reason-
able at the commencement, as their condi-
tion at the close forced them to be. Ws
do not, however, wish to criticize too
severely the conduct and proceedings
of men at a moment . when they must
be suffering through the vexations of
discomfiture. We simply urge considerations
on them which we believe will benefit 'them
if they attend to th stn. We urged them also
at the commencement of the struggle, but
without any effect whatever. Still it is our
duty to protest egainst damaging mistakes;
to condemn in working men what we should
disapprove of in men of any other class ;
above all things to press upon them the duty
of acquiring power by entering into union
with each other; And the duty also of using
this power moderately and fairly. There
are other points in. this struggle upon which
much might be said. In its settlement the
question of overtime was not wisely dealt
with, nor was the time of leaving Work on
Saturday judiciously arranged. But if the
defeat suffered has the effect of carrying the
men into their union the ultimate gain will be
more than any present loss, though it must be
confessed that the shock of this disaster is
likely to be injuriously felt wherever the
labour struggle is carried on.

LLOYD JONES.
PRICE ONE PENNY.

Ip. I.
STANDING AUMIES AND THE AUTUMN

MANCETPRES.

IT is scarcely to be expected that the masses
of the people who have so recently come. into
the possession of political power should at once
comprehend their political position and pre-
pare themselves to use their power in mph a
way as to be most serviceable to the general
community. There has not yet been time to
arrange an understanding between our liberal
working people and the liberal men belonging
to
,the other classes of the nation. Common
principles are needed, and if a common policy
can be outlined no time should be lost in com-
pleting so exoellent a work. At present those
who ought to be taking the lead in organizing
a great Liberal party are groping in the dark
distrustful of each ether, and but very dimly
conscious of the great, and important work
which, notwithstanding all that has been
done, still remains to be accomplished. .
In social and industrial economy, as well as
in politics, there would be no difficulty. in
naming a great number of questions to; which
public attention might profitably be direoted.
The men who attended the teeent political
gatherings at Cannon-street, thrashed the
straw, no
,doubt, lustily, and certainly
knooked a groat deal out of it, but they-Aid
not succeed in getting all it contained. They
got too much to be useful as .the basis of a
great party, but not enough as matter ade-
quate to the exigencies and.requiremeuts of the
times. It would be difficult, nay impossible,
to unite a great party on such a raultitnde.of
subjects as those put
,forward in the Cannon-
street programme; but there is not one of
those subjects which working. men ought not
to investigate, and, if possible, thoroughly
understand and seriously take to heart.

The indifference of the masses of our work-
ing people to questions pf absolutely vital
interest is almost bewildering, and some of
those questions, which, from their import-
ance, ought scarcely ever to be absent from
working men's minds, are as a rule least
thought of. -Permit me, as an instance, to
bring one of these questions under thnnotiee
of your readers. Take the ease of "standing

employment, and the wasteful expenditure
connected with them in every way. For
fighting purposes each nation keeps those
almost innumerable legions of men called
" standing armies." As machines for murder
their construction is marvellously effective.
The expedition and certainty with which they
kill cannot be too much admired. But is it
not a pity that so many able-bodied men, who
might be turned to good account, should thus be
taken away from employment in useful work,
and is it not deplorable that so many millions of
money earned by hard toil should be abstracted

support? ,

In addition, moreover, to the maintenance

army and a

I CANNOT, in justice to myself, but more
capecially in, justioe to the system of indus-
trial partnership with which the firm df
"'HENRY. Bnioas and Co. (Liniited)" is-
'identified, allow the •comments of Mr. LLOYD
JONES in your paper of Saturday, August 24th,
• to pass without,in a few Words, seeking to put.,
your readers in possession of the actual 'facts
of the case on which Mr. JONES 'dilates with
such vehement eloquence, and to vindicate the
corirse' of ,aCtion Whioh he assails with such
fierce invective. With respect to unionism,
the benefits Of which Mr: Joiis estimates at
such a high value, I am not prepared: to deny
that the colliers have reaped some good there-
rom ; but I am bold to assert that whatever
may have been the advantageous results of
colliers' unions, the policy of such associations
has often been inimical to the real interests of
their members, and- the ruling spirit of their
councils hit been, -and continues to be; one
of antagonism to their masters. The System.
of industrial partnership has been originated
and sustained by our company with the object
• askr. JONES acknowledges, of uniting masters
'and men in the bonds of sympathy; and in
the attainment of mutual prosperity; and
thereby as the natural consequence tending to
do away with the occasion and necessity ' of
any union amongst either masters by them-
selves, or men by themselves—to act on behalf
of their own class • interests regarded as alien
and contrary to each _other.
• In working out our oo4perative union,
between masters and men, carrying with it all
. the benefits of union amongst the men by
themselves, yea, and tenfold more, and none
of their evils ;. we have been careful to avoid
doing anything byword or not, indirect
or positive, in opposition to the miners' union of
our district. Having faith in our system, we
have relied on the men learning to appreciate
its benefits, and thence withdrawing from
unions against their masters, to be more
thoroughly in union
.with them, Pursuing
• this course as most fitted to gain acceptance
for our system, we have refrained from inter-
- feting with the union so long as its-leaders did
not seek to tome between us and our men, and
thus frustrate the vital object of industrial
'partnership.
Hitherto, unlike some of our neighbours,
we have never prohibited our men from join-
ing the union, and no man has over been dis-
missed our employ solely because, he was one
of its members. When, however, we find
the union direotly assailing us; when non-
union men are—that they may lead a quiet life.
and escape from being blaekguarded and
dubbed blacksheep—driven.against their con-
victions to subscribe to union funds; when
our best men are foully abused and insulted
by union men for working too hard, and

getting too much coal; when meetings for
propagating union sentiments and beating up
recruits are started at the pit bank instead
of the men starting to work ; when we re2.eive
a notion from men in our employ stating that
they "intend to o" to a union demonstration
on the very day of our annual meeting, at
which a bonus of £5,250 on the workmen's
wages is proposed to be voted by our share-
holders, then I felt that it was high time to
take a decisive Step, and by making the in-
timation, which has loused the ire of Mr.
JONES, let the union know ouse for all that
the management of our collieries was not to
be taken out of our hands, and our pits made
to play at our behest. Our men had
,thus
furnished them a fitting opportunity, after an
experience of some 'years, to choose between
Co-operation, with its bonus in addition to
the wages of the district, find the Union, with
.C22,,000 of its funds spent on strikes.
M. DIXON writes of the Meeting in Leeds
as being a "day of pleasure," the "one day
in the year ;" but it is notorious that it was
a union demonstration, and the union
speeches constituted the main feature of
the entertainment. Our men had. their day of
pleasure end annual trip, the "one. day in the
year," on the 6th of July, for the cost of which
they had not to subscribe by small instalment
out of their wages, the expenses being defrayed
by the company. ,
Mr. Drxor confidently asserted that if the
men attended the Leeds meeting they would
consequently work with more alacrity and
steadiness. The working of the men who
went to Leeds has given the, lie to Mr. DixoN's
sanguine prediction. Three-fouttlis of them
were idle on the Tuesday, one-half of them
On the Wednesday, and not a few on the
Thursday. A very different effect was
wrought on the energies of those who attended
the meeting of workmen held on the evening
of the same day as the demonstration in the
company's wagon building shop, when the
CHAIRMAN warmed their hearts by declaring
the amount of bouus,to be paid on the wages
of the past year. '
Mr. LLOYD JONES is very groat on tyranny,
but I am utterly at a loss to ace where the
tyranny was, in giving men the choke of co-
operating with us and receiving bonus, or being
on the sam.e footing with their neighbours in
the union, but without bonus. In further
vindication of the course I deemed it right to
take, and in which I have been supported by
our board 'and shareholders, I may We 11 ask
what would these latter have thought, had
they, on coming to our annual meeting at
Whitwood, found our pits standing, that men
to 'a horn they were about to be asked to vote
over £3,000 in hard cash out of the profits of
the year, might attend a Union demonstration
in Leeds, whilit at adjacent non-co-operative
pits the colliers were in full work earning
profit thrown away by our employs. Would
they not have been justified had they in their
honest indignation and disgust at such sham
60-operation refused to pass the resolution
with respect to bonus, which I, the tyrant
held up to ignominy and scorn by Mr. JONES,
proposed?
I need not, I should think, add another
word to defend myself from the charge made
against me by Mr. JONES of having struck a
deadly blow at the interests of co-operation,
which was clearly, by the decisive action taken,
saved, as far as. our company is concerned,
from imminent peril 7 but would just let your
readers know what it.is our present intention
to do with respect to the union.

It is not our intention to decline to employ
union men, or to establish a rule that no union
man is entitladtobonus ; but our directors, sup,
ported by the shareholders, have determined
that union men who persecute their fellow non-
unionist workmen, or seek at any time to stop
the working of our collieries, shall quit our
service, and, that all who in spite of our plain
notice loft their work on the 19th of August,
though they have the bonus for 1872, will not
receive it for the current year.

With a view also of taking away from our
men the only justifiable reason which they
have for being members of the union, viz.,
the advantage derived from the benefit fund,
we are on the point of originating a similar
fund in connection with our own collieries,

and loTards this fund purpose to ask our
shareholder's to vote a handsome amount.
Incidentally, I ma 3r remark that our A.eri-
dent Fund is universally admitted to be the
most liberal in the -district.

I am glad to be able to assure all who may
glance at this letter, which has' already
reached too ,great a length, that our workmen
as a body are ,amongst the inostaitdustrious
and intelligent in West Yorkshire, 4nd if we
can by (Air unfailing exideavour -restue those
Who wish to be 'independent co-operative
workers with us from union sophistry and
thraldom, and foster the spirit which during
the last three weeks has stimulated men to
apply for over three hundred of our shares, we
,may safely leave results to determine whether
the union of labour in antagonism to capital,
or the ,union of capital and labour for the
'achievement of a Common good, is the most
Wind, improving, and widely heneficiil
system.

On Sunday morning the second of a series
of meetings which the London Patriotic
Society is convening in various parts of the
metropolis, was held on Clerkenwell Green,
for the purpose of taking steps to prevent a
continuance of the existing prices of provi-

Mr. Pottle presided.

That in the opinion of this meeting the causes

people in excess of supply, and the want of suffi-
cient protection to the farmer for his investments
in the land required to increase the agricultural

waste lands of the United Kingdom. That we

LONDON.
TECH WINS WEAVEES.
To the Editor of the BEs-Htvt.
San—We, the wire-weavers in the employ of
Mr. F. W. Potter, of Barbican, were this morning
agreeably surprised by a spontaneous act of
liberality and justice which sots a good example
to the generality of employers. We were informed
that, from the present date, our wages would ho
increased 5 per cent., with extra pay for over-
time to the extent of 10 per cent., making a total
advance of from 3s. to 4s. per week.

We are desirous of making this public, as it ap-
pears a more just and a better method of grappling
with the labour question than that so generally
adopted, and which, unhappily, appears to be on
the increase at the present time, namely, strikes
and lock-outs.

We are convinced that, as a matter of policy,
masters would find it advantageous to take the
initiative in these matters instead of opposing the
reasonable claims of their men till compelled to
yield. Not only would strikes and their number-
less attendant evils be avoided, but a considerable
advantage gained by the substitution of mutual
confidence and good feeling for mistrust and
animosity.—Hoping soon to hear that many others
have followed Mr. Potter's example, we are, Sir,
your 'obedient servants, for the weavers in the
employ of Mr. F. W. Potter,

Barbican, Sept. 4.

This council held its monthly meeting at the

ing, the president, Mr. Thos. Clay (mason), occu-

vice-chair. The secretary read the minutes of the

Several members then testified to the already

beneficial influence. It would draw people closer

On Saturday evening an important conference
took place at the Town Hull, Macclesfield, between
silk manufacturers and delegates from the Weavers'
Trades Union with reference to a demand made
by the latter for the abolition of the charges
hitherto made against them for the entering,
twisting, and turning on of their warps. The
demand bad been the subject of a previous con-

that tho trade prospects at present were so gloomy,
and foreign competition so great, that the present

was a most inopportune time to burden the manu-
facturer with further expenses. The weavers had
decided to use all legal means to obtain the ad-
vance they now asked for, which, at the most,
would not be above four per cent.
Mr. Nicholson, on behalf of the manufacturers,
stated that at a large. and influential meeting of
that body they had unanimously decided that they
could not afford to give the advance.
At the end of the meeting, however, Mr. Chap-
man having stated that this advance, if conceded,
should settle the trade so far as they were concerned
for " some considerable time to come," the mann-
facterers promised that if the delegates at a future
meeting would name a time during which there
should be no further agitation the masters at a
fnture meeting would further consider the question
with such a condition appended to it.

BIRMINGHAM.
TILE SIIOE3fAKELLS.

On Tuesday night a meeting was held in the
Temperance Hall, under the auspices of the Bir-
mingham Rivetters and Finishers' Association, for
the purpose of hearing an address from Mr. George
Odger, of London, to trades unienists, and to con-
sider the advisability of "instituting a Federation
of Trades Unions in the Midland Counties."
Mr. Jeremiah Thomas occupied the chair.
Mr. Odger urged that it was by combination
that they would better their condition, and in-
stanced Stafford as a proof of this, where there had
been a good combination, and wages had gone up
during the past twelve years 40 per cent. At
Leeds, also, since the late strike, in some cases,
there had been an advance of 40 per cent. lie
advised the shoemakers of Birmingham to get
similarity of wages all over the town. Ho spoke
in favour, of Boards of Conciliation aud Arbitration
between masters and men, counselled thorn to
always approach their employers in a kind spirit,
and said he believed many of the employers desired
to advance them if it lay in their power. He was
almost ashamed to find in this glint town that
there had not been more combination amongst
them, and thought Birmingham men should look
to it. The combination he proposed was not to
injure"molest, or destroy the prospects of any
body of men, but to support what was right, to
sustain what was just, and to be sure the work-
man should share in the prosperity of our common
country.

On the motion a Mr. Juggles (secretary of the
Nut and Bolt Makers' Society at Darlaston),
seconded by Mr. Newby (electro-plato worker),
the following motion was then passed
That this meeting deems it necessary to the in-
terest of labour, that there should be some means
adopted to bring about an amalgamation or
federation of all trades and labour associations in
Birmingham and the district surrounding, so that
each union may receive the assistance of other
societies in case of any dispute with capital.
A resolution was also carried giving power, to
the executive of the association which convened
the meeting to invite delegates, so far as possible,
from each trade, for the purpose *of framing such
laws, &c., as might he deemed necessary to be
placed before a future meeting of the delegates.

articles.title: TOBACCO PIPE MAKERS.
articles.text:
THE TOBACCO PIPE MAKERS.

The following memorial having been sent
.te
the master tobacco pipe makers of London, and
its terms not having been conceded, the men are
out on strike, and say they mean to remain out
until they get the terms asked. The men in their
memorial say,—We wish most respectfully to bring
before your notice the present state of wages of
the journeymen tobacco pipe makers of London,
and, further, to show you that the present wago
are totally inadequate to supply us with the com-
mon necessaries of life. You are doubtless aware,
gentlemen, that we hold an inferior position,
financially speaking, to the most common labourer
of this country. You are doubtless aware, also,
of the enormous rate at which rent, coals, and
provisions are rising, and also of the rapid increase
of wages in all other branches of industry.
Therefore, gentlemen, in common justice to our-
selves and families, we lay before you a scale of
wages that is consistent with the emergency of
the present time. It will be observed from the
resolutions herein contained that a uniform rate of
wages throughout London is sought for. This
has been done with the view of dealing out justice
equally to both masters and men. We also wish
to call your attention to the fact that the employers
of Scotland have conceded to their journeymen an
extensive rise of their wages. The provinces are
also following their example; Northumberland,
Cumberland, Westmoreland, Durham, Lanca-
shire, Yorkshire, Nottingham, Birmingham, Bath,
Bristol, and other places too numerous to mention,
have already gained a considerable advance; and
it gives us pleasure to state that the majority of
questions have been settled without resorting to
strikes. We wish also to bring under your notice
the fact that during the last thirty years our
wages have decreased about twenty. five per cent.,
and that provisions, have risen at about the
same rate, so that we are fifty per cent. worse off
than formerly. Surely, gentlemen, this fact alone
will suffice to show the justice of our petitiou.
Taking into consideration all circumstances, we
believe that journeymen were never more justified
In makiug an appeal ,to their employers for en
advance of Wages than we are at the present
time.

articles.title: – THE LONDON BUILDING TRADES.
articles.text:
- THE LONDON BUILDING TRADES.

There are two well marked dates in the
history of the past dispute, that seem to
exhibit a want of calculation on the part of the
majority of workmen, while demonstrating to
the full the practical results of the three
months' struggle. On the Bth of last July
the masons returned to work under an agree-
ment, stipulating that for 40 weeks in the year
they should work 9 hours on Monday, 91 on
Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday,
and 51 on Saturday, at 81d. an hour, or
£1 17s. 21d. per week, and for the 12 remain-
ing weeks 81 hours on the first five days, and
41- on the sixtli, at the same rate orl 13s. 31d.
per week. On Monday, Sept. 2, the carpenters,
bricklayers, plasterers, painters, and smiths
began work, upon precisely the same condi-
tions, with the exception that on Saturdays in
the second or winter division of the year they
will work an hour more, making their wages
140., per week, instead of £1 13s. 31d.
The joiners "in shops" will work 521 hours a
week all the year round. It will thus be
seen the masons, "the cream of the trade,"
who were the first to discover the expediency
of effecting a compromise, come nearest to the
terms of the memorial, viz., a working week
of 51 hours. On the other hand, they have
abolished "systematic overtime," by the
observance of a long-established custom that
has obtained the force of law just as much as
a written agreement, and in this respect per-
haps they stand upon a better footing than the
other branches.

TILE CARPENTERS.—On Monday their central

The Committee have issued the following work-

including half-hour for breakfast, and one hour

for breakfast.

The working hours on out-door works to be 62i
hours for 40 weeks in summer, commencing
and leaving off the same time as joiners in shops,
and 48 hours for 12 weeks in winter, commencing
every morning at 7 a in., and leaving off the first

The standard rate of wages to be Sid. per hour
all the year round.
Overtime, when worked at the request of the

The first hour at 9id., and from the end of the
first extra hour until 8 o'clock p.m at the rate of
per hour; after 8 o'clock, Is. Old. per
hour.

The above rule not to apply t 3 the case of men
working overtime at their own request, or to
make-up time lost during the week.
On Saturday, time and a quarter up to 5 o'lock,
and time and a half after. Night work to be
subject to special agreemeat.
All wages to be paid at the time of leaving work
on Friday.
At a conference held by the sub.-committee of
the Master Builders' Association and the car-
penters aud joiners on Tuesday, August 27, 1872,
it, was unanimously resolved, on the motion of
Mr. Hannon, seconded by Mr. Makin :
In the opinion of the sub-committee of the
Master Builders' Assooiation and the deputation
of carpenters and joiners now met tmether' it is

Signed on behalf of the Centrai jommittee of

C. MATKIN, Secretary.

THE BluestAmis.—On Friday, after several
hours' palaver :the bricklayers' deputation ac-
cepted the terms concluded with the other
branches, and succeeded in getting tacked on to
them some additional provisions which custom had

already sanctioned. The agreement or me-

2, Westminster Chambers, 30th August, 1872.,
At a conference between the Sub-Committee of the

The working hours to be 62i for forty weeks in

On Monday night a meeting of the bricklayers

Mr. B. Coulson, general Secretary cf the

established the basis for a code of working rules
a thing the trade had never had in the London

made, both by society and non-society men, to
have it generally adopted by the master buildera
of the metropolis. Me concluded by moving,

That this meeting receives arid endorses the
agreement its to working hours and rates of wages
come to between the sub-committee of the Ceram'
Association of Master Builders and the deputation
from the Operative Bricklayers' Society, and
pledges itself to use pvery legitimate moans to

Mr. Fisk seconded the resolution, which met

stuck out for the "nine hours and the ninopenoe
pure and simple."
Mr. Batchelor and other members of the depu-

A remeuntative -of the bricklayers of Perry and

of the Society were to make a representation the
new terms would be immediately granted all
round. The men would gladly place themselves
at the disposition of the society.

Mr. Batchelor thought it would be bettr in the
first instance that the men themselves should make
the appeal to the flan, and if it failed then the
Connell of the Society might take the matter in
hand with other similar MEM At present, how-
ever, the Council had come to a decision as to the
steps to be taken to compel the employers outside

terms.

A vote of thanks was passed to (ho deputation,
and a similar compliment to the chairman for

hour.

Tun A NI ALO MATED TRADES C OMMITTRE.—A

Several meetings of the journeymen have been
held during the week, and the strike committee
have issued the following manifesto :

ArPHALt TO TUB rumw.

FELLOW CITIZENN—In this enlightened age
actions of men must harmonise with public
opinion, and in appealing to this tribunal to pass
judgment upon the bakers' dispute, the operatives
feel that the verdict will be upon the side of truth
and justice and in their favour. For years past,
as the world is well aware, the condition of the
journeyman baker has been a disgrace to his
employer, a shame to humanity, and a scandal to ~
civilization. Education, science, and philanthropy
have achieved much for all other classes, but in
his 'ease they have done little or nothing. Ile
is still the outcast of the industrial system, the
Pariah of the social circle, the only artisan who
is deprived of. his rest, denied his Sabbath, and
doomed to toil iii confined dungeons, the fo3!.id
atmosphere of which is as fatal to life as the
poisonous breath of the Black-hole of Calcutta.
Government inspectors have denounced the evils
surrounding him as most baneful and demoralis-
ing; and medical men hays affirmed that he is a
prey to the most debilitating influeneess and his
term of life the briefest of all classes—in a sen-
tence, that he is murdered by long hours and ex-
cessive toil. For him there is no respite. his
existence is that of a dog. He scarcely knows
what it is to enjoy a night's repose. His sleep is
a 'pitch' in the heated bakehouse, his bed the
board upon which the bread is made, andavhen
he rises from his hard couch his sweat and tears
literally • mingle with the ingredients of which
the staff of life is manufactured, and which the
public are compelled to eat. The Sabbath comes,
but comes no Sabbath day to him, and thus, year
after year, be drags out a. miserable monotonous
existence, labouring 10, 18, and '2O Fours a day,
at a wage which a sweep era scavenger would ro-
flop, until his health fails, and a-pretnature death
terminates, his sufferings. Will any Christian
man say that the .operative baker ought to he
satisfied with such an iniquitms system? When
all other trades are Obtaining increased pay and
reduced hours, is he alone to be condemned to
sleepless nights, excessive toil, low wages, disease,
and death? Certainly not. Itis his duty as a pro-
gressive being to china a share of the advantage
which all other classes enjoy ; and, as the. Times
justly says; "if his demands are.not unreasonable
and can be conceded, they ought to be." It was not
the journeymen's wish t 6 have taken the initiative
in the work of /darn. They preferred the masters
should have taken the lead, but the employers
declined the task, and advised,
.before they could
take any actienin the mattern that the men should
be united and he ready -with a platform to con-
stitute the basis for discussion. The men heeded
the advice, fused themikelvis into one central

organization, and prepared a platform of principles;
but the masters, instead Of calmly diseatssing the
matter with them, treacherously broke faith and
substituted one of their own; Still, as the first
principle—the working (14 Of twelve hours from
four to four—was retained intact, the men sub-
mitted to the indignity, and amended their plat-
fortn to meet the Masters' views. But they were
no • better Off even with: the concession. The
masters at their next meeting cancelled the only
proposition Upon which their own coittnitte-e and
the men were agreel, and pledged their delegates
to a 'series of resolutions which they kite* the
operatives Could not :accept. We now come to a
conSidPration of thO 'two platforms. The men
gay We require a ivorking day of 12 hours, the
time of which shall be Eked from four to four, and
a recognised minimum scale of wages."' Surely
there is nothing unreasonable in this demand.
But the eniployers. say "No: •We will give you
a day of 12 hours, or 72 per week ; but the time
shall not be fixed. It shalt be left to the require-
ments of each partiettlaf shop." A more Sestiitictd
evasion could not rbe Conceived. By InsiSting
upon this condition they know they will per-
petuate the " any " 12 hours system which for so
many years has wrought ruin and degradation
upon the trade. "The requirement of each
'particular shop "is a. very elastic phrase. It
;means that there shall be no uniformity; that
employers shall have the right to make what
stipulation they. please; that those in certain
distriets'sball dein' night work at half the wages
given for it in others. Against such a principle
the men must cOntehd to the bitter end. They
may be vanquished, as they are poor' and their em-
ployers are rich, but better they Should be reduced
to dock labourers and scavengers than silently
submit to h bondage more 'degrading than that
which the Egyptians imposed upon the Israelites.
Between bondage and starvation there is little
seepo for choice;' but of the two it is better to
die from want than to linger on a miserable ex-
istence in slavery, a curse to ourselves, and
accursed by our fellow mon. We have, however,
faith in the great heart Of humanity, and in the
agony of our sufferings we venture to appeal to
our Countrymen and countrywomen. We appeal.
to trade unionists to support our humble efLrts to
obtain those boons which they already enjoy. We
appeal to the religious sttntiment of the community
to demand for us that Sabbath which should be
held too sacred either to be bought or sold. We
appeal to that love of fair play which has over
distinguished the English press at times like these,
and trust that its potent voice will be heard in our
behalf, and lastly, we appeal to the general
public, whose sympathies are :ever on the side of
right and justice. Let it: not be recorded in
history that in this the 191 century, in England,
the home of opulence and prosperity, a pcor de-
graded class of artisans were 'allowed to be yoked
to the serfdom, honause they had not the sinews
of war to fight against the capital of their
merciless employer. :
By order of the London Council of Operative
Bakers.

PETER POLE, }
Secretaries.

340TTINGS OF A D*IiiTTA'I'ION TO

LANCASHIRE.

But Lancashire prospers and trades unionism
flourishes, to the chagrin of those acute reasoners
who have so conclusively demonstrated the utter
impossibility of such a result. There is something.
to learn every day if ono will kcep his eyes open,
and one of the most conspicuous facts of late
years is the lie which practice has given to
theory.

When the agitation for a reduction. of the hours
of labour was first fairly put before the public by
the building trades:.of London some fourteen
years ago, the doetrinaries came out in very strong
force. Adam Smith, Ricardo, McCullock, were
invoked, and jt host of other smaller fry, but their
illustrious names to prove the utter absurdity of
the workman's claim and his Stupidity in believing
lei. a. moment that ho' could influence by his. action,
eithertbe hours of labour or the rate of wages.
Supply and demand, and po'itical economy, were
as unerring in their operation as time and tide;
and neither the eloquence' of Demosthenes, or the
strength of Hercules could succeed in thwarting,
for one motnent,the operation of those greatnateral
laws. So universal was this chorus that the
workmen, half .doubting,, succumbed, suspecting
that in his ignorance he might have stumbled into
a mistake, and set to work to "read u " in poli-
tical economy. But tho hard sehool'of experience is
the place to learn the facts of life, and certain
laird facts seemed irreconcilable with the theory,
that if everything is left to itself all will come right
and equitable. The increase of. crime and pauper-
ism on the one hand, and the increase of luxury
and indulgence on the other; the mass of the
workers increasing in poverty, while the non-
workere increased in wealth; the many glaring
psaraples of largo employer's netting their fortunes
in a few years, and living in retired andstately
mansions, while the workmen's lot seemed to got
harder, and the moat prudent found it difficult to
make ends meet.

These were not considerations likely to make a
man contented with the "open your mouth and
shut your eyes and see what God will send
you" principle; and so, leaving political economy
to look after itself, he persistently resorts to
demands for shorter hours and more wages, and
the result is that from one end of the country to
the other, from the makers of buttons to the
builders of ships, chorter hours or higher wages
more or less prevail, and the Government has so
far been influenced by the tendency of the times,
that after fixing railway fares and buying up all
the telegraph companies, proposals are now on foot
for the purchase of the railway system and the
regulation of gas works and water supplies. Lon-
don is about to be introduced to a system by
which the size and description of pipes, eis •
terns, taps, &c., are regulated by an order of the
Board of Trade. Why this interference with
saleable commodities, if things will naturally
right themselves between consamer and seller P
It is true these facts do not prove that the law
o' supply and demand does not operate, or that
political economy ifs a false doctrine, but rather
that certain great facts have been left out by our
learned friends in making their‘. calculations, just
as a mariner setting sail for some distant shore in
ignorance of certain• strong currents which cross
his path finds himself drifted on a flora he had
not contemplated. It might be a very desirable
thing if the days were all one length, and the aim
would uniformly shine; but if the great fact of the
shorter days of winter were not provid'ed for by
artificial light, we should find ourselves in the
dark, whatever our wishes or desires might be.
And so if the workman can by any means estab-
lish certain great facts in relation to his position
in society, or the terms and
.conditions of working
in his trade, politiesl economy will] have to take
account of them, or so much the worse for political
economy. It sounds very grand and convincing
to hear the long-drawn deductions from "great
natural laws.". But a little reflection will show
that there is a deal of fallacy in crediting nature
with too much perfection.
The whole scheme of civilization is nothing
more nor less than an interference with great
natural laws. human nature tends to eavagery,
and human institutions to barbarianism, and it is
just in propoition as man reetricts his natural
impulses or the laws of eociety check the tendency
to evil that we advance or retrograde. Look at
the beautiful show of prize flowers; they were
once nothing more thal weeds. Of the rosy and
luxurious display of fruit it comes of a once
wild and det,rioratedsto,k. The marvellous siva-
mens at horticultural exhibitions--they all owe
their perfection to the fact thut by the ingenuity
of man they have been trained 'and cultivated
out of their natural btute ; and so Cs With the
pros,ras of society.

A government to be worth anything m oat be to
the people what a trade unionist would under-
stand by an executive of a society, under the
supervision and control of a General Council or
Parliament, whose paramount duty should bo to
deal out even-handed justice to all its members
alike, without caste or distinction. Any measure
which favours an individual or class at the expense
of another is the very essence of injustice. We
hear a deal of cant about contentment and
freedom, as ,though freedom consisted in every-
body being allowed to do as they like, and not a
principle to be regulated by circumstances, and the
capacity for exercising it without injustice to
others. •

The model of contentment is a fat 'pig, and the
freest individual on earth is the Mirage. Ile is at
perfect liberty to work, or play,_ eat, drink, or
sleep. lie may rob or kill his neighbour if he
has one at his pleasure, and no fear of detection
disturbs his slumbers, or punishment await his
waking. Absolutely free and unfettered he does
as he likes. It is fa very easy matter to have too
much individual freedom, and so think the staunch
trades unionists of Lancashire. In Rochdale, for
instance, no member of our craft is allowed to
work many hours unless he holds a card of mem-
bership of some trade society or other, or at once
promises to join one. This will be thought sharp
practice in London, where they enjoy so much
freedom and se few advantages, and I cenfess it
jars On Our susceptibilities having always held the
opinion that
.a malt has a perfect right to join a
society or not, just as ho may think fit. Although
I have always felt that the arguments of those
who contended that for trade purposes non-society
aro as good as society then, 46 not hold 'water.
Assuming that it is conceded, a watchfulness is
necessary in trade .matters to protect the interest
of the workman. It is -difficult to see how the
man. who neglects theordinary precautions against
trade emergencies or the means of keeping up a
supervision and constant Check on the ,abuse, of
the employers' power, can be doing his duty so
well as the man who acts on the opposite, any
more than the citizen who never votes or takes
any interest in public affairs, discharges his duty
so well as his neighbour" who acts on the contrary,
or that the rude untrained civilian is as good a
man for his business as the practised professional
soldier.

And, moreover, no one can deny the right of
any body of men to object if they please to work
or play, or in any way live or be connected with
men whose conduct they believe to be detrimental
to their interests. But inversely suppose that in a
place like London, for instance, where not more
than 25 per cent. are society men, the non-
unionists were to net on the same rule, and object
to work with unionists. Here would be a com-
plication not contemplated :perhaps by our Lanca-
shire friends. The fact is, that questions of this
kind cannot be fairly decided on abstract prin-

both sides.

The case of the trades unionist has never been
fairly recognised by society, neither can it be.
But there is no doubt that the fact of

so constantly misrepresented, persecuted, and
maligned, has led to a spirit of reprisal on his part,
and especially in cases where his detractors have
been his fellow workmen. Trades unionism . is a
species of religion which strikes its roots deep into
a man's conscientious convictions—it appeals to
his sense of right and wrong, and affords a seope
for the exercise of the hest instructs of his nature;
its leading features are unselfishness and
mutualistn, and no man can be a good unionist
whois not willing to sink his individuality for the
general good of his fellows. All the doctrines and
supetstitious dogmas that have from time to time
been tacked on to Christianity, are as nothing coin.
pared with the grand admonition, "As y
would that men should do unto, you, do
ye even so to them." Religious expounders have
failed to 'see this feature in
.working moos'
organizations, and consequently religion has be-
come a class institution shunned by the workman
on account of its unreality, and followed by the
wealthy and genteel on account of its elasticity;
and while we have . had histories of the pilgrim
fathers, the Huguenots, and every species of
religious and political persecution, the trades
unionist, with his ardent hopes and aspirations,
receives but a rasing and contemptuous refer-
ence, and no historian attempts to do jubtice to

tion. The offer of the SPEAKER to receive
deposits from his labourers as investments ill
his farming business, guaranteeing 2- per seal
andtdding as much more as the profit mad°
will allow, is not very revolutionary ; nor 14,,
it to be supposed that labourers, move'

whom the highest and most exceptional wages
is 15s, per week, with a family in most oases
no doubt depending on it, can save much
as a trading investment, whatever bait of high
interest may be held out to them. Neverthe-
less, the offer of the SPEA.KEIL indicates a
loosening of old ideas and 'a breaking up of
old habits. It carries in it an assurance that
things cannot go on in the condition in which
they are, that somehow they must be changed;
and such an assurance in regard to the con-
dition of the agricultural labourer foreshadows
changes of an extraordinary character in
regard to the future condition of labour in
England.

The SPEAKER, in reply to supposed objectors,
stated that capital is neither more nor less
than labour husbanded. A very old dogma
amongst political economists, but it is almost
new as an:argument in favour of labourers'
right of investment in the land they till. May
it not, however, find a wider interpretation,
and may not all active labour be regarded as
conferring claims of interest in the work in
hand whether husbanded or not? Why
should not the worker have an interest in the
result of the labour, which he exercises day by
day to produce this result in a given proportion
*to the man who investshis money, but who could
not make that investment profitable were it not
for the labour whose co-operation gives it
safety and causes it to yield a profit?

Mr. BRAND'S scheme is not a showy one, and
it was brought forward and explained in a
thoughtful and modest way, quite creditable
to its proposer; still it has more value in it
a thousand times over than those see-saw
sentences of Lord DERBY, which are as useless
as they are impartial, which, in fad, have no
value so far as the practical work of the nation
is concerned. His well-balanced utterances,
like soap bubbles, are all that can be desired
in form and colour, but like these they dis-
appear and leave nothing of any value behind.
The SPEAKER'S project may not lead to much,
but it will produce some practical good. It
offers itself as a remedy so far as it goes; and
that in the present situation of the country, as
regards our agricultural labourers, is a matter
about which wo have some reason to feel
pleased.

articles.title: LONDON WITHOUT BREAD.
articles.text:
LONDON WITHOUT BREAD.

TuE strike threatened by tile journeymen
bakers of London naturally excit 35 a wide, a
household interest. What, says Materfamilias,
shall we have no bread? In answer to this
question of anxiety and cry of alarm, we find
ourselves constrained by the progress of daily
facts to say, that, from meetings of men held
in all parts of the metroplis, there comes but
one voice and one word, " Strike ! " It remains
to be seen, whether the volume of sound is
sufficient, the emphasis of the utterance strong
enough, so to impress the minds of the recalci-
trant masters as to supersede the necessity for
pushing matters to that extreme. Hitherto
their reply has been the proposal of a con-
ference between masters and men. By this
means, and this means alone, they assert, can
the questions on which the two arc at issue be
settled. The proposal, no doubt, has the
appearance of fairness and of conciliableness ;
and, for the time, the men, who decline it,
seem thereby to put themselves in the wrong,
or, at least, into a position of disadvantage.
But what has to be considered is, whether the
proposal has the reality as well as the semblance
of being fair, and whether it has been offer ed
to the men in such a form and under such
circumstances as.to make acceptance morally
binding or wisely politic on their part.
Well, they have not been deterred from
carrying their case up to the Court of the
whole bread-eating public. This, surely,
shows perfect confidence in the justness of
their appeal. In language which shows either
that knoaders of dough can handle the pen, or
that they have friends among those who are
good at that implement, they ask the whole
world to say whether their condition has not
been for years a disgrace to the employer, a
shame to humanityrand a scandal to civiliza-
tion. There is the true grip of force as well
as the leaven of truth in language like this
The journeyman baker, say they, is worse off
even than the dustman, the sweep, or the
nightman. Each of these has his seasons of
cessation and of rest but the ;nen who leave

loaves at our doors are still the outcasts of
industry, the pariahs of society, without beds
and without Sabbaths, doomed tq dungeons as
fatal to life in the long run as ever the Black
Hole of Calcutta. Let it not be said that all this
is so much phrasing. " His term of life is the
briefest of all classes " that is a fact or it is
nothing. He is called upon to labour for be-
tween sixteen and twenty hours a day,
including the seventh—is that true or false?
But why strike? Why not confer? They
never wished to take the initiative. They
waited for their employers to do that. They
have waited long and for nothing. "Unless
they spoke up for themselves, who would
have taken up the cudgels for them? They
have now taken them up, for themselves, and
they do not mean to lay them down until some-
thing like justice has been extorted by their
resolute attitude. Those very masters who
now pretend to say, Come, let us reason to-
gether, first cast suspicion upon their own
sincerity in the use of words outwardly pacific.
Lay down, they said, a platform for discussion,
and we will meet you upon it. The challenge
was accepted; when those who offered it, drew
back, and would consider nothing but a plat-
form of their own. What faith, say the men,
can we put in proposals for conference after
that? Nevertheless, as the principle of a
twelve hours' day, from four to four, was left
intact, the men
.submitted, and met the
masters' views. What ensued upon this ?
The masters, at their very next meeting,
cancelled the only proposition on which there
had been a material agreement, and, for the
rest, imposed upon their delegates conditions
which they well know the men would reject.
The masters will no doubt reply, that they
adhered to the day of twelve hours. Yes, but
with this important limitation, or, as the men
say, "Jesuitical evasion : " the twelve hours
shall be distributed from day to day over the
whole twenty-four, according to "the require-
ments of each particular shop! " An arrange-
ment so elastic would be open to numberless
inflietions of gross injustice and oppressive
hardship. To name but one, masters in one
district could, under it, be enabled to demand
nightwork at half the wages paid for it in
others. In fine, "against such a principle
the men must contend to the bitter end; "and
having so announced their determination, they
leave all the world but master bakers to judge
whether they are not in the right.
The" West-end bakers," however, are those
only, or at least those chiefly, whom it is
necessary to challenge
•as unfit to sit on this
national Court of Appeal Those "gentlemen
bakers" say that their customers must have
hot rolls every morning; and this, they pre-
tend, 'cannot be, unless their men are at work
earlier than four o'clock. This is the first
time we understood the denizens of Mayfair to
be such early risers. We had a notion that
breakfast by eight o'clock was altogether an
East-end demand, and that, at the opposite
quarter of town, it was deemed soon enough
to crawl out of bed when the sun had touched
the meridian. If, however, we may credit one
of the speakers for the masters, an early supply
of hot breakfast bread is absolutely essential
to meet the demands of their largest and best
customers—the keepers of hotels and similar
places. "if," says this person, "they did
not bake the bread at the convenient time
for the hotels, and for those other people
who wanted it at a certain hour of the morn-
ing, there would be plenty who would at once
step in and take their trade away from them.
It was all very well for the journeymen to ask
the four to four system; but the masters must
study the position and exigencies of their
trade. They had as yet only looked at the
subject as one between the master and the
journeymen, but there was another party to be
considered, and that was the public. If the
public had acquired a certain taste—if it
desired rolls at five o'clock in the morning, it
would have them; and, if the West-end trade
were not prepared to supply its wants, the
public would obtain it from the East."

Now, to say the very least of it, this presents
a new view of the morning habits of the com-
fortable classes. Never before were they pictured
to our mind's eye as engaged by thousands in
munching hot rolls soaked with butter at five
o'clock all the year round. But, to speak on

a serious subject in a serious manner. We
would not accept the responsibility of advising
the men, however ill-treated, and, as they
allege, deceived, to cripple their own freedom in
negociation by perseverance in such terms as
"the bitter end." Nor, on the other hand
let the masters, at one end of the town or at
the other, imagine that it rests with those to
shuttlecock-and-battledore the quegtion be-
tween themselves. Let both rely upon it,
that, unless they find the means of establish-
ing peaceful relations with those whom they
employ upon a basis mutually satisfactory,
their whole trade, except in tarts and hot
rolls, might some fine morning take wings and
leave them. Nothing in all the world would
be easier than for the country millers and
other large dealers in flour to supply all
London with daily bread on terms of great
advantage to themselves, and in all probability
much easier to the general body of consumers.
Let a word to the wise be sufficient.

articles.title: WOLF AND THE LAMB.
articles.text:
THE WOLF AND THE LAMB.

IT is very amusing to notice the way in
which the fable of the wolf and the lamb, as
illustrating the conduct of colliery owners and
working colliers, is unconsciously repeated day
after day in the columns of our daily papers.
Employers and their friends have been so
habitual in their complaints of the conduct of
working men, awl have so frequently covered
their own wrong doings by censuring them
that they seem quite unable to understand any
putting of the case which does not place the
men in a wrong position. This habit of the
employers and their friends has had a very
injurious effect on the public mind, so far as
the proceedings and interests of the men are
concerned. Whatever takes place as a dis-
turbance of trade always, at first, gets
explained to the public from the employers'
point of view, and it is only when the contest
is prolonged and third parties take an interest
in it, that the men can be fairly heard at all.
This coal question is just such a ease. At
first the excuse for the advance in price was
solely attributed to the advance in the price of
labour. If the men in any district or any
colliery when they saw ss. a ton added
to the selling price asked for an ad-
vance equivalent to threepence or four-
pence, an outcry was at once raised that this
demand of the men was the sole cause of the
advance. The public, knowing no better,
believed in this knavish allegation ; trades
unions and agitators were forthwith roundly
denounced, and the coal-owners and coal-
dealers divided the spoil with an admirable air
of injured innocence.
In an.artiole which appeared in the Times
of Tuesday last this old game was played
off in a very skilful manner. There was a
mixture of independent thought, as if the
writer was an uninterested onlooker, with a
carefulness of arrangement in figures and
statements which put the poor colliers greatly
in fault as compared to coal-owners, and at
the end an attempt at scientific statement as
to our coal resources, good enough in itself,
but when all these were taken together, the fin-
pression left was very unfavourable to the
proceedings of the working men in the coal and
iron trades. When the article, however, is read
carefully and its true meaning sifted out, it
proves most conclusively that enormous sums
of money are at the presett moment being
extracted from the pockets of the public under
pretence of necessities which do not exist, to
create the fortunes of persons whoee chief
merit is that they know how to plunder, and
who have just now an opportunity to do so,
many of whom will, in a few years, place
themselves before the world as meritorious,
self-made men.

At the opening of his article the writer in
the Times furnishes a number of figures,
which, if put together differently from the
way he has placed them, tell a very curious
tale. Last year steam coals ranged from 10s.
to 103. 6d, per ton, this year the same coal
ranges from 255. to 275. ; household, last
year Os. to 12s. per ton, this year 245. ; last
year gas coal Bs. 6d., this year 225. to 23L;
and so on over the whole list, though the
figures are not in all cases given. This rise
taken on the whole output of the pits of Great
Britain, with an average advance in price of
loth per ton, will give, to be divided. amongst

coal-owners and dealers in one year, no less a
sum than sixty millions sterling, not as a tan
profit, but as an extra profit. This is a pretty
heavy fine levied by these gentlemen on the
community, but the evil does not end here.
This is simply the first instalment. The rail-
ways, being injuriously affected, have raised
their rate for carriage of goods, which the
public must pay. Fares for passengers must
follow. In fact every person who uses coal in
the public) service for private profit will follow
suit, and so the game of plunder will go on so
long as the screw can be made to turn in its
pressure on the consumer.
What have the men got out of this? This
question ought to be repeated over and
over again till some kind of answer be
given. We say less than 6d. a ton at
the outside. If they get more, let the clever
writers in the Times, and in the other
daily papers, make it clear, knowing, as they
do, all about this coal question. With figures
at their. fingers' ends they could make the
matter plain without any trouble. Why,
then, do they not do this ? Our explanation
is that they want to charge the working
colliers and trades unions with it, and if they
made the true figures known, they could not
do this. Still they ought to tell the truth, if
for no better reason than that given by " Hot-
spur "—that the devil may be shamed.

articles.title: WORTHY OF CONSIDERATION.
articles.text:
WORTHY OF CONSIDERATION.

A SUGGESTIVE article on the Bakers' Strike
in the Spectator last Saturday calls for com-
ment, not so much in consequence of any
statement of fact, or any argument it contains
relative to the action of the men, or the.
merits of the case, so much as in consequence
of a speculative argument towards its close as
to the right of the public, or the Government
as representing the public, to coerce any body
of men, bakers or others, whose action might
endanger the general welfare of the corn-
raunity. The abstract argument is illustrated
by suppositious cases, but the drift of the
writer is plain enough, and the object be aims
at not to be mistaken. What power does the
public possess over a trade or a class?
Should that trade or class, in pursuit of a spacial
interest, put the general interest to an extreme
risk? Suppose, says the writer, that "all
merchant sailors struck at once for impossible
terms so that Great Britain was virtually in
blockade ?—or that all policemen struck for a
pound a day ?"
In such cases, it is argued, that it would be
justifiable to use force for the purpose of
compelling these men to do their duty on
reasonable terms in the interest of the com-
munity. This is justified on the plea that
the " right of the State to exist is higher than
the right of the individual to be free, and
this right of the State the Spectator declares
to be more perfect in a free country than
in one despotically governed. If, however,
such a state of things as that supposed by our
respectable contemporary is never likely to
arise, so far as working men are concerned,
it would
.be simply a waste of time to argue
it in relation to them. A universal sailors'
strike cannot occur, and if it did, im-
proved terms would soon break its force by
destroying its universality. Policemen are
not likely to strike for a pound a day, and if
they did, we imagine there would be no great
difficulty in supplying their places for a trifle
less. If the bakers make a strike that may
temporarily interfere with the bread supply
of London, there would be little difficulty—
time being given—in meeting such a state of
things. The old women of the north of Eng-
land manage to keep up the weekly supply of
bread without troubling the bakers much about
the matter, and in London the old women could
easily do the same thing. We shall, therefore,
admit the force of the Spectator'B argument,
and grant all it looks for as right on the
part of the State to protect itself against the
mischievous action of individuals or classes of
individuals. We do not deny it, but we ask
for its application where an actual, not a sup-
positious, danger exists. It is always better to
assert and to argue a principle in connection
with what is or what may be, than in refe-
rence to what is not, and what is not at any
time likely to be. We shall, therefore, dia.-
miss the question so far as bakers, sailors,
policemen, or other bodies of workers are,

concerned, and apply it to classes and interests
whose proceedings already threaten the safety
of society, and who, therefore, in accordance
with this strong doctrine, call for a restraining
action in the interest of the general com-
munity. Let us take our great landowners,
and see what their doctrines carried to an
extreme would lead to. The Duke of SUTHER-
LAND we know, at the commencement of the
present century, in the exercise of his rights
as a landlord, depopulated a county. His
agents deported men to make room for sheep,
and subsequently made the sheep give way to
deer, that his estate might yield a larger
profit to the proprietor. His right to
do this wait vindicated by publie writers
at the time, and altogether the doctrine was
stoutly- maintained that a man has a perfect
4, right to do what he likes with his
own," At the present moment, land-
lords and farmers between them have so
•narrowed down the labourers' chance of
existent*, that an exodus of labour i 8 setting
in, which •fromises, at no very distant time,
to leave our fields atad villages bare of men.
The tendency of property, every day
creasing in power,is to squeeze out labour ; to
force it to find a new home across the Atlantic,
or Wherever else it may be able to take itself
to. The Sutherlandproprieter made his cal-
culation, and found sheep and deer—in a
pound, shillings, and pence sense—better than
men; BD the menhad to clear out.. But when,
during the Crimean. warrthe .9,unnN wanted
subjects, and the nation -soldiers) none could be
found in Sutberlandshire, and therefore a
foreign enlistment
,Act had to be passed, and
an attempt made to crimp men in America,
which led to an ugly embroilment with that
conntry.

Now Lord DERBY and other landlords and
farmers arc going in for machinery, or any-
thing else which may lead a peasantry who
will no longer starve in quiet to emigrate,
But then soldiers will bo wanted Again ; and
conscription is already talked of. That is,
our landlords are to have the privilege of
forcing the labourers off their estates by with-
holding from them the means of a decent and
comfortable life, and then of compelling the
other classes of the community to defend them
from attack should their safety or property be
threatened.

This is, we think, a little too bad ; and hero
the doctrine of the Spectator will be found not
only practicable, but sound and wholesome.
The working men of the country who are
interested in each, other's welfare, who count
now for something as a power in the State,.
must see that the safety of the country and
the welfare, of its people must be protected
against the dangerous action of dominant
classes and interests. There is in the state a
right of coercion—a right to preserve itself--
and this right must, when necessary, be
enforced against our upper classes and in
favour of the masses of the people„ We
thank the Spectator for laying down this
doctrine, and we hope to bee it recognised
and acted on by the people whenever called
for by the requirements of the nation. Lord
DEnnY, who cautions the labourer?, hints at
tillage superseding cereals and other food crops,
should labour boom° too dear, but the prin-
ciple laid dowaby the S'peotator, and sanctioned
by the old practice of the country, may find
very efficient legal remedy for that—a remedy
which will go on the old principle that, a man
- cannot always do what he likes with his own,
and that what he frequently calls his own
with a very loud voice is held by him rather
in trust for the welfare of others—to be used,
not abused.

THE SPEAKER AND CO-OPERATION.

MERE is much pregnancy of meaning in
the interpretation which JESUS CHRIST put
p on one of his own parables,—that of the
steward wlio, to make friends with his master's
debtors when he was threatened with being
thrust out of his stewardship, wiped out half
of each man's debt without having received
the money ancl without any authority from
his offended employer. The act was unjtlfit
but then, it was shrewd; and as the C+,11,13.0!
Tslcuilt remarked, the children of this
world are wise in their generation. Not all of
them, however, are always. It %till() ago

thing for "the children of this world," and for
the whole world besides, when they acquire
the faculty of loOking some little distance
before them, and the wisdom and, resolution to
make arrangements in prudent and sagacious
anticipation of coming events casting their
shadows before. And there is ,so great force
in example, that all have reason to rejoice and to
hope when a good example is set from a conspi-
cuous eminence. On these grounds, we haiLwith
satisfaction, and not without expectation, the
measure taken by the &TAKER of the House
of Commons with respect to the managetnent
of his own estate.
.The late events in War-
wiekshire, and in some other counties, have
not, it is evident, been thrown away upon the
mind of Mr. Ilium). No sooner had he been
liberated from the labours of. h long session
than he applied himself to the task of setting
his, own house in order.
The celebration of the harvest -home at
Glynde furnished him with the finest pos-
sible occasion for. announcing. his consi-
derate intentions to those most interested .in
them; and also to the whale 'agricultural
public. In the first place, the in-gathering of
the fruits of the earth had proved excellent,
and abundant; and, to borrow anOther sacred
expression, 'they who sowed and they who
reaped, as Mr. BRAND determined, should
really rejoice together. Three years . ago he
made up his mind that he would pay no 'wage's
to youths till they should be. both able to read
and Write. Wu dare say it was Vary plain to his.
own mind that the complete propriety of this
step must depend Upon other steps which
accompanied or should follow it. For our own
part we have repeatedly insisted that the
labourer is, all the world over, worthy of
his hire; that the ancient maxim not in,
muzzle the ox which treadeth out the corn, IS
one of which huroan threshers have a right to:
share the benefit, that, indeed; as the. best
authority, next to CIIRIST himself, lays down,
"the" husbandman that laboureth," neither the
owner who farms his own estate, nor the
farmer who occupies it at stated rent," must
be first partaker of its fruita ';" and that, as
the most practical of all the SAVIOUR'S
Apostles. contends, "the labourers who have
reaped down" the fields, not merely have the,
first claim upon the owners of those fields, but
have a claim which GOD himself expects to see
,
fully satisfied, or, if net, then let those who
fail in this duty "weep and .howl for the
miseries that shall come upon them." The
course whiclithe S vEA KER,IOt one, has announced
makes it evident that consideration' s of this
order have taken firm hold of his mind. His
predecessor spout much inoney and rains in
the completion of what is known as "The
Speaker's Bible." It is the happy distinction
of the .gentleman who has succeeded to that
high office to conform his own actions to the
,declared principles
.and precepts of that book.
His words on the occasion are 'so truly golden,
and it is so important that the example which
he has set should be made' widely and fully
known, for. the 'stimulus of men_ of his
.own
rank and position as well as for the encourage-
ment of those men of another rank and posi-
tion, Whose very means of subsistence aro at.'
issue in
,the matter, that we shall give to ,
those i'verds,.as reported, the utmost publicity
and prominence we can.

articles.title: PARENTAL RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES.
articles.text:
PARENTAL RIGHTS AND
RESPONSIBILITIES.

FACIOEY operative at Staleybridge has
Vindicated, and successfnlly asserted the'right
of the poor man no less than the rich to the
possession, control, andlirection of the edam-
education of his own child. By order of the
local School Board, JONATHAN SCHOFIELD was
served with notice to send liii little girl to
school. He answered calmly by standing upon
his parental authority. The reply of the
Beard was, that he had not urged a "reason-
able, excuse" for non-compliance with its
order. He was therefore called before the
Board, but declined to appear. A sum-
mons was then taken out, in accordance with
Which attended before tho n3agistrates.
The questions there raised were, first, whether
he Was qualified to instruct his daughter;
secondly, whether he really did instruct her.
As to SCHOFIELD'S ability, -their Worships
might have been satisfied. by the, intelligence

and self - control which he manifested
throughout the proceedings. It was proved,
however, by the testimony of several
competent witnesses, among whom, we believe,
the Rev. JOSEPH RiYNEIL STEPIIENS was one.
The second question was satisfactorily met
by the little girl herself, whose answers to the
magistrates as to reading, writing, and arith-
metic were such as completely satisfied them,
The Bench, consequently, ruled that she was
under efficient instruction, and dismissed the
ease. "I claim the right," the father said in
his defence, "to have and hold my own little
girl, to keep her on my own hearthstone,
under my own roof, there to have her so-
brought up that, if she should in after life be
sought by another, as her mother was sought
by me, she might be to that husband what her
mother has been to me, a loving, obedient, and
happy English workman's wife. I will not
insult you, gentlemen, by imploring you to
refuse to give your sanction to the allegement
that the statute before the court was designed
to enable gentlemen to use ,their mansions as
schoolhouses and prohibit labourers from
teaching in their lowly cottages."

articles.title: TIIREA.TENED STRIKE IN TIIE LONDON BAKING TRAD.
articles.text:
TIIREA.TENED STRIKE IN TIIE LONDON
BAKING TRAD.

LOOKED at altogether there is no trade where
ameliorating influences require more to be
called into operation than in the baking busi-
ness. The manner in which journeyman
bakers are used, as a rule, is a disgrace to the
country, and in some way or othot efforts
should be made to shorten their bouts, and
in general to improve their condttion. The
first duty in this matter tiles with the em-
ployers. From their deliberatiens ought to
come some sound practical remedy which the
men might accept, and it may be added that
any settlement pared now by the employers
should ge so far in the direction of the men's
demands as to prevent for as long a time as
possible any ,recurrence• of the present dis-
turbance. A twelve hours' day is in all con-
science long enough, nay, considering the
direction in which things are moving, it is too
long. When, however, in addition to this,
these hours are looked for night or day, it is
difficult to see how any great improvement can
be looked for, as the want of uniformity in the
hour of work must inevitably lead to other irre
gularitios which in a very short time would de-
stroy all uniformity, and bring back the oppres-
sive irregularity in the custom of Work, which
already exists. If a West-end baker finds it
necessary to supply his customers with hot
rolls at early morning hours, and if this
cannot be done without running counter to
what the trade generally desires to see estab-
listed Lis a custom, let the double-shift system
be resorted to, and night raen and day men
between them get through the work, if it must
be done. The old saying is true here—
" Where there's a will there's a way," and
makers and men should seek honestly and
earnestly to find this out.
To the men we council moderation; baking
is a skilled trade, but it is a trade not difficult
to learn ; household baking is a very common

which future improvements in the trade

venience of strikes. .
