articles.title: CONGRESS OF THE INTERNATIONAL.
articles.text:
THE CONGRESS OF THE
INTERNATIONAL.

The delegates to the Congress of the Inter-
national Association at the Hague having ar-
rived, a private and informatmeeting was held
on Sunday evening. Amongst the delegates
present were M. Karl Marx, secretary for
Germany and Russia; M. 'Engels, for Spain
and Italy; General Wroblesky, for Poland;
M. Serillier, for France; M. Leo Frinkel,
for Austria • and Hungary; M. Conrmet, for
Belgium and. Denmark; Mr. M'Donell, for
Ireland; Mr. Harcourt, for Australia ; Mr.
West for the Philadelphia Congress; M. Sogre,
for the Gorman section of the American Intev-
nationalists ; M. Saura, for the French seotion ;
and Mr. Roche, for the London General
Council. Mr. Hales, general secretary, was
also present. The Congress will extend over
Saturday, and finish up on Sunday night.
The police seem well informed of the move-
ments of the delegates, meeting them at the
station here and conducting them.to the head-
quarters of the International.
On Tuesday, as on the previous day, the
sitting of the Congress of the International
Association was secret.

There is a rumour that difficulties have
arisen in verification of the credentials in con-
sequence of certain members fearing they
might be exposed to trouble from the autho-
rities as condemned criminals, having con
cealed their real under false names, which are
also used in their credentials.
The verification of the credentials of the
delegates is at length concluded. The diffi-
culty with the Spanish deputies is arranged by
admitting them. On Wednesday the point in
controversy was with respect to the section of
twelve delegates from New York. This section
is composed chiefly of adherents of Mrs.
Woodhill, of free-love notoriety. After an
animated discussion, verification was refused.
At night the meeting was occupied with
arrangements for the sittings of the Congress,
which are to be public to-morrow. There is
little doubt that the Centralisation party will
carry the day.
During the secret Session next morning the
Chairman stated that ho had received infor-
mation that agents of the French and German
police are here watching the movements of
the delegates. -

articles.title: CANTERBURY CATHEDRAL.
articles.text:
CANTERBURY CATHEDRAL.

The grand old Cathedral at Canterbury had
an alarmingly narrow escape from
.total de-
struction on Tuesday. At one period of the
greatest danger it was feared that the whole
of the upper portion of the noble edifice wo.
become a ruin, so tierce was the conflagration.;
but, happily, owing to the really heroic
exertions made by the fire brigades, military
police, and general public, the flames were
stayed, and the destruction limited to the roof
of the eastern end of the building. The fire
was first discovered shortly after the conclusion
of the morning service. The organist and
choir were at rehearsal, when a messenger
rushedinto the Cathedral, and announced
that names were issuing from the roof at the
east end. The alarm was instantly given to
the Cathedral authorities in the .Precincts.
Mr. Superintendent Walker, of the county
police, was also informed of the circumstance,
and he at once sent to different parts of Kent
for a large body of police, and in a very
short time they, with a strong body of city
police and 150 soldiers from the barracks,
arrived on the scene. The latter were provided
with the barrack engines. The hose of the
local agencies of the County, Phcenix,
and Kent Fire Offices were also brought
into requisition, and the Volunteer Brigade
lent -their willing help. While, however,
plenty of means were then at hand for play-
ing upon the fire, the want of sufficient water
supply within the Precincts greatly jeopardised

the initiatory 'efforts that were being made to
get the fire -under. In order to overcome
this difficulty, the hose were run through
several private grounds, to reach which it was
necessary to break through the Precincts
boundary wall. All this entailed much delay.
There :were many murmurs among the rapidly
increasing throng of spectators against the
Dean . and Chapter for not having given to
their valuable property the advantage of the
city water supply. At length, however,
sufficient store was obtained to begin playing
on the flames, for lofty as the roof of the
building was, some 100 ft., the pressure in the
mains was sufficient to reach it. By this time
the flames had got well hold. of the roof above
Trinity Chapel, and were gradually advanoing
westwards towards the junction of the choir
with the eastern transepts. Fortunately
the whole of the interior of the building
is groined, so that the fire was confined to the
woodwork composing the outer roof. Another
circumstance also favoured the preservation
of the edifice. The roofing over the eastern
end has not, like other portions., been repaired
since the sixteenth or seventeenth centuries;.
and the massive well-seasoned timber of which
it was composed did not fall so ready a prey
to the devouring element, as would have been
the case with the pitch Pine woodwork which
has been introduced into the restored parts of
the building: Still, it was slow work to make
an impression on the flames. Not more than
two or three hose could be dragged to the
great height, and the danger was also greatly,
increased by the vast amount of molten lead
which 'poured off the roof of the building. So
great was the danger from this latter circum-
stance, that . more than one person narrowly
escaped being scalded. The metal ran down
the vaulting and boiled over the outer walls,
.streaming down the buttresses like a brilliant
, shower of corruscated silver; It also found its
way through the opening of the bosses which
hold the interior of the groining, and. dropped
like liquid fire into the chapel below. One
stream coming from this source bespattered the
mosaic pavement at the foot of Thomas b.
Beoket's • shrine. The armour of the Black
Prince, which 'hangs over the Prince's tomb
within a few feet of the same spot was removed
by the direction of the Vice Dean. The
Cathedral authorities, fearing that the groin-
lag might yield to the pressure of the fire above,
also removed the altar Cloth and all that
could possibly be got out of the 'choir, even to
the Communion rails and the pulpit lining.
This alarm was not entirely groundless, forat
one time the choir was fall of smoke, and the,
boiling lead and water streamed into it in many
places, though fortunately not in sufficiently
large volumes to do even so much damage as
was done by those who got out all that was
moveable. The actual work of the fire was
confined to the outer roof, and the flames were
entirely subdued by one o'clock. The extent of
the damage coVered an area of about fifty feet
long, including the apse or Trinity Chapel, the
most eastern' portion of the edifice. Beckett's
.Crown, which is virtually separated from the
body of the building, was uninjured, and the
elegant screen at the rear of the altar also
escaped damage. The afternoon service was
held in the choir at four o'clock, when, except-
ing that the drugget was up and that the altar
rails had not been replaced, the building in
other respects presented its usual appearance.
special anthem and" Te Deum " were offered
in acknowledgment of the gratitude' of the
oongregatiop. After the flames had been ex-
tinguished refreshment was offered by the
Dean and Chapter to all who had taken part on
the occasion; • and the military mustered and
were publinly thanked by the Rev. Arch-
deacon Harrison, of Maidstone,' for their
valuable services. The damage done by fire
is roughly estimated at .t 4,000.
The firemen displayed considerable courage
in taking up positions on the roof close to the
flames, from which they directed streams of
water with excellent effect. Much anxiety
was felt as to the interior of the Cathedral, but
by the active exertions of the firemen the
valuable relies were remoied without any
considerable injury. At one time the saddest
forebodings were entertained as to the ultimate
fate of the building, its complete destruction
being at one time considered probable' but by
half-past twelve the flames were 'got under.
About three' quarters of the choir roof was
totally destroyed. The damage to the interior
of the building was fortunately trifling, con-
sisting of the falling of showers of molten
lead on to the mosaic pavement in front of
Becket's shrine, which, however, is not in-
j'ured. The fire is believed to have wiginated
from a charcoal pot which some plumbers had
been using in the repairs of the' roof. The
damage is covered by insurance in the Sun
Fire Office. In order not to deviate from the
custom of daily service, which has been
maintained for 300 years, a special service i
was performed at four o'clock n the after.
noon, at which Archdeacon Harrison: prefaced
the prayers by 'a few words, urging those
present to offer special thanks for the pre-
servation of the edifice. Canterbury Cathedral
has suffered from fire on former oceasions,
the last previous to that now recorded having
been on the '6th of September, 1174. It is
stated that orders had been given for bringing
, the water within the Cathedral Precincts.. ,

articles.title: SPEAKER ON CO-OPERATION.
articles.text:
THE SPEAKER ON CO-OPERATION.

The Right Hon. the Speaker of the House
ot Commons gave his annual treat to the
labourers on the Glynde Estate, to celebrate
the ingathering of the harvest, on Saturday,.
:The right hop. gentleman presided' at the
,dinner, and, in reply to the toast of his health,
proposed by the Vicar of Glynde (the, Rev. W.
de St.. Croix), he congratulated those present
upon the abundance of the harvest in that
part of the country, expressing his regret that
all parts of the kingdom had not been similarly
favoured. The right hon. gentleman con-
tinned: It will be in your recollection that
about three years ago, when we assembled in
this tent, I callecl the attention of the young
boys in my employ to the necessity for those
who could not read and write, and who wished
to remain in my service, to-learn to' do so at
once; and I warned them that unless-they did
they would not continue in my service. lam
happy to find that that warning has produced'
'a good effect, and I intend to adhere to the
principle that all boys who wish to be em-
ployed by me must, learn to read and write
before they can receive wages. Now I suppose'
that in these times, when there is so much
talk about the rate of wages, yon will hardly
think I am doing my duty if I do not say some-
thing in reference -to the agitation which is
going on throughout the kingdom. My opinion
is we shall never have a satisfactory settle-
ment of that question until the labourer
receives in some shape or' other a share—
though it may be a small one—of the profits
of the business in which he is engaged. I
refer not only to those employed upon farms,
but to those engaged in mining, in manu-
factories, and in trades of all kinds. But you
will say, how is the labourer to derive any
share of the profits of farming, because he
has no capital? Well, it is quite true that you
have no capital beyond' your labour. But
what is capital? Capital is nothing more nor
'less- than labour husbanded. Now, if you
could save any money, however small the
amount, and could invest it in carrying on a
farm, 'think, according to the sum so invested,
you would be entitled to a share in the profits
of that farm. (Hear, hear.) I will give you -a
practical illustration of what I mean. Some
of you, I daresay, are fortunate enough to
have a few pounds in the savings bank, and I
believe the savings bank limits the interest
paid on the investment ii to 21 per oent. Now,
I will make a proposition to you and all in my
employ. If you have got £5, we will say, in,
the savings bank, and you would like to lend
that to my farming business, I will engage to
give you as the savings 'bank does, 21 per
cent. for the money. And I will do more than
that. I will, supposing the profits of the farm
amount to more than 21 per cent, for the
money I -have invested—l will give you
rateably precisely the same interest upon the.
capital you lend me: (Cheers.) That is to say,
supposing I get 10 per cent. as profit- on the
capital I have invested in the farm, you shall
have 10 per cent, on your £5, instead of 21;
(Cheers,) So that you will be in this position:
that you will never get less than 21 per cent.,
which you receive at present; and if the farm
yields more you will have the benefit of it.
Some will ask, How am I to get the £5?
Well, we know it does not rain £5 notes, but
I will suggest to those who have' not got that'
athunt in hand that they should lay by so
much a week. The rate of pay to the boys is
from 3s. 6cl. to 4s. a week and the wages increase
according to the ability to work. The carters,
shepherds, ao., for instance, receive about 15s.
per week, and out of this it seems to me it is by
no means impossible that some may save 2s a
'week; and, if you pay me that sum, I will
engage at the end of theyear to pay you the
£5 if you desire it, plus 21 per cent., or what.'
ever rate of interest arises from the year's
farming operations, I am-quite sure of this,
that we shall never come to a satisfactory
settlement of the relations between employers
and. employed until the latter, according to
the amount of labour and capital he has
invested, has an interest in the good conduct
of the concern (Hear, hear.) My solo
object is to give you a personal pecuniary
interest in the conduct of the farm, and to
endeavour to raise you a little above the
position you now ()croupy as labourers. (Loud
cheers.) -
The propositions were afterwards: favour.
ably discussed by the men:

articles.title: ALEXANDRA PARK.
articles.text:
ALEXANDRA PARK.

THE LORD MAYOR'S CORRESPONDENCE
WITH THE PRINCE OF WALES. 7:

MANSION HOUSE,
LONDON; E.G., 16th Aug., 1872.

Si;-

I feel that it is scarcely needful to convey ta
your Royal Highness my profound. assurance that
nothing • but a matter of more than ordinary
importance could induce -me to trespass on your,
time and attention.

There are occasions when individuals in every
station of life may combine for the purpose of
effecting works of public utility, which,
without such combination, would not be accom-
plished,

The work in which I seek to interest your Royal
Highness is
.a cum in point.
A critical epoch exists in the social history or
the country in reference to the so-called recrea,-,
tions cif the people, and the effect of those recrea-
tions on the physical and moral condition cf the
industrial classes. It is especially true of this
section of the inhabitants of London, numbering
probably not less than two millieins, that with
scarcely an except'ontheir amusements are of a kind
which appeal to the grosser passions of humanity
degrading and demoralising those who participate
in them, and making each succeeding generation
leas capable of performing their duties as Christians
and loyal subjects.

The knowledge of these things makes it
apparent that recreation of a pure, refining, and
invigorating kind should be provided in .every,
available quarter as a counterpoise to these terrible
evils.

My magisterial as well as my private ex.
perience has taught me that if the choice of good
and of evil be offered to the people, tliey will
reje,et the bad.
A committee of noblemen and gentlemen has
been formed with the object of securing the
Alexandra Palace and the beautiful Park of 500
acres, and dedicating the Institution to purposes
of pure and healthy recreation. The preservation
•of this noble expanse is of paramount importance
to the health of the metropolis, for immediately
south of it lies a portion of the City nine square
miles in extent, wherein is &tamely an acre of
clear land on which the pent-up toilers can breathe
and iecreate free from the vicious temptations
which unfortunately encompass them.
The object of this letter is to acquaint your
Royal Highness with the proceedings whith I
have instituted to remedy, in some small degree,
this state of affairs ; and I enclose a report of a
public meeting recently held here, and the resolu-
tions which were then passed.

Agreeing with the sentiment expressed by your
Royal Righness's lamented father, that it is our
duty to individually exert ourselves to further the
accomplishment of what we believe Providence tb,
have ordained; and believing, as I do, that it is
ordained of Providence that men and women
should be blessed with vigorous bodies and sound
minds, I have set in motion the movement, which
the committee agree with rue in thinking wili
materially promote a reform of the existing evils.
With this explanation I bog, with the utmost
respect, to ask your Royar Highness's approbation
of these proceedings ; and if, at the same time, I
might be favoured with an intimation that your
Royal Highness and Tier Royal Highness the
the Princess will honour the inaugural ceremony
with your and her presence. Such intimation
would stimulate the committee to increased
exertions, worthy of your Royal Highness's
commendation, and wonld virtually ensure the
complete success of our labours.—l have the
honour to be, &c.,
(Signed) Sit,Ls JNO. ChenoNs.
ilis Royal Highness the PRINCE of WALES,
&c., dco.,

MAULBOROI.7OII ifOITSE, PALL Mau., KW.,
31st August, -1872.

MY LOUD,-

I am desired by the Prince of Wales to thank
you for the communication IV hi c h be has received
from your lordship respecting the purchase of
the Alexandra Park.

His Royal Highness agrees most cordially with
the sentiments expressed by your lordship on the
subject, and he will be prepared, when the proper
time shall wily°, to give his best consideration te
any application that may be made to hint' to be
present, together with the Princess, at the in-
augural ceremony.—l have the honour to be, my
Lord, your lordship's most obedient 's rrant,

(Signed) FRANCIA KNoLLys, Private Secretary.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

The new Licensing Act is being enforced
with rigour in some parts of the metropolis.
In the Clerkenwell police district nearly 70
publicans have been summoned for infringing
the early-closing provisions. At Highgate on
Monday the bona fide traveller question came
before the magistrates. Two licensed
victuallers were fined for having opened before
the legal hour on a Sunday, and penalties
were also inflicted upon those who mil)
drinking in the houses at the time. In the
City, after the passing of the Act, a few houses
received the special permission of the Police
Commissioner to keep open.until one o'clock
in the morning. It is now, however, an-
nouneed that "after 'due inquiry and oareful
consideration," it has been decided not to
permit any licensed premises to be open after
midnight.

In the Bankruptcy Court Mr. Registrar
Pepys granted continuance of an interim in-
junction in the case of Mr. Strange, proprietor
of the Royal Surrey Zoological Gardens, to
protect the property from execution until the-
creditors met. No opposition was made; and
it was stated on behalf of the receiver that,
contrary to damaging reports which had been
spread, the Gardens were not closed.

An ex-constable named Storey, who is in
receipt of a pension of £1 per week from the
police funds, has been committed for trial on
a charge of robbing a City firm, by whom he
was employed as night watchman.

A salutary example was set to railway
travellers at Greenwich Police-court the other
day, where an elderly man named Lambert
was fined ss. and costs for leaving a carriage
on the London and Brighton Railway before
the train had been brought to a standstill at
the platform.

Herr von Lutz the Bavarian Minister of
Public) Worship, has resigned, and there NOIII
shortly be an entire change in the personnel
of the Cabinet.

Djemil Pasha will bo replaced as Turkish
Ambassador at Paris by Safuet Pasha, who
quits the Ministry of Justice.

Illustrating the proverb that calamities
seldom come singly, the disaster to the Ameri-
can steamer Metis, which hurried some sixty
or eighty souls into eternity, has been fol-
lowed close by another catastrophe, attended
also with heavy loss of life. Tim steamer
Bienville, from New York to Aspinwall, was

extinction was resolved upon, met on Monday
evening. A resolution was passed calliDg on
the manager and directors to resign.

Two female servants employed at the Duke
of Cornwall Hotel, Plymouth, have been sent
to prison for three mouths for stealing a
number Of articles, chiefly provisions, from the
hotel. The thieves were detected by tho
diseovery of a parcel of plunder which con-
tained a note to' a friend, with whom,
apparently, on the strength of their intended
present, they invited themselves to take tea.

A collision took place on the Lake of
Zurich, a few days hack, between the steamer
Gothard and the Concordia, from Meilen,
carrying, on an excursion of pleasure, all the
pupils of the public schools of that town.
In fifteen minutes the first-named vessel sank,
but the passengers and goods were saved by
the other, which was able to reach the shore.
The purser of the latter was drowned.

An attempt having been made to corrupt
and get rid of a man named Miller, who is the
principal witness against the three men now
in prison charged with murdering John
Wien, at Wishaw, the man has been appre-
hended, and will be detained till the trial. A.
large sum of money and a -free passage to
America for himself and family were offered
him on condition that he would set out forth- .
with.

The Lord Mayor has received through Mr.
Childers a remittance of £B5O, from the
Mayor and committee of Melbourne, Australia,
on behalf of the fund raised for the relief of
the sufferers by the famine in Persia. A
further sum of £250 is prOmised.

In the case of Messrs. Gleilstanes and Co.,
an application was made in the Court of Bank-
ruptcy on Wednesday for the extension of the
injunction. The liabilities are very heavy,
being estimated to be between £1,500,000 to
£2,000,000. The failure is attributed to
losses on home and foreign consignments, and
no one appearing to oppose, his Honour ex-
tended the injunction until the farther order
of the court.

The Marquis of Bute is rapidly recovering
prom the serious effects of the accident he
sustained recently. On Tuesday afternoon
his lordship, accompanied by the Marchioness,
drove out for about an hour. This was the,
first time Lady Bute has been outside the
castle grounds since her recovery from illness.

Of the Metropolitan' Benefit Society's
Asylum, at the eighty-fifth half-yearly meeting
of the members, held at the Portugal Hotel,
Mr. H. Palient in the chair, two inmates were
elected out of a list of 14 candidates. The
report showed the expenditure for the half-
year to be £275 175., against receipts £367
Os. ad., leaving a present capital of £6,787
14s. 7d.; and an urgent appeal was made for
further funds to allow a fuller development of
the institution. The asylum, which is situate
in Ball's-pond-road, Islington, at present
contains 48 inmates who are severally pro-
vided with a furnished room, coal, gas medical
attendance, and an allowance of gas,
()I,a
week; their average age being about seventy-
two years.

Three French soldiers on sentry duty at
Narbonne have been insulted and attacked
with stones by a group 0160 persons. Ten
persons were arrested, and their trial ill
take place in a few days, when A is expected
that severe sentences will be passed. The
soldiers attacked belonged to a regiment
which repressed the disturbances at Mar-
seilles.

George Leak, a plasterer, has been crushed.
to death at the Chartered._ Gasworks, having
been caught by a strap and dragged into the
machinery.

At the Surrey Sessions John Armstrong
has been sentenced to seven years' penal
servitude for breaking into the convent
schools attached to St. George's Roman
Catholic Cathedral, Southwark, and stealing
therefrom 26 muslin veils and other articles.

The Junior Army and Navy. Club will
shortly Move into the premises lately occupied
by the European Assurance Society, in
Waterloo-place„ Pall Mall, opposite the
Athenamm Club.

Mr. J. J. Barrett, a tradesman in Pentonville•road, has died suddenly in consequence
of over work. 'rwo months ago his medical
adviser recommended him to take a holiday,
but ho declined to do so. The post modem
examination she wed that the cause of death
was an effusion of the brain, brought on by a
weak heart.

The Countess of Loudon has replaced the
swoo of Wallace in Loudon Castle, from
whence it had been taken by the late Marquis
of Hastings to England a few years back.

Michael Davitt, a Fenian prisoner, writes
from Dartmoor Prison to the Dublin papers,
complaining of the cruel manner in vOl4
he has been treated in prison.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

A band of Mormons, numbering COO, sailed
from Liverpool on Wednesday for Net York,
en route for Utah.

News received by Reuter's agency from
Gibraltar, states that the. passengers crew,
and cargo of the French, mail steamer Panama,
which was wrecked in Santander Bay, were
all saved. • •

During a thunderstorm at ,Lisk card on
Wednesday the telegraph-room of the post-office
there was set on fire by lightning. The coils
and lightning conductor in a needle instru-
ment were completely fused, and even the
brass-work was melted. The lightning passed
on to a gas-burner, scorched the pipe, and set
lire to the gas. Telegraphic communication
with the office was suspended for some hours.
The first arrival of foreign bops, the growth
of 1872, consisting of two bales of Alost of
good colour and quality, have been yesterday
received by Messrs. James Preston and Morris,
hop merchants, Southwark-street, Borough.

The executive committee of the Interna-
tional Exhibition having offered a selection of
raw and manufactured cotton for permanent
exhibition at the Peel Park Museum, Salford,
a resolution was passed at the meeting of the
town council of that borough on Wednesday
accepting the offer, and authorising the chair-
man of the committee and Mr. Plant, the
curator, to proceed to London to make a selec-
tiOn of specimens.
Colonel Wilson-Patten has announced his
intention of giving £3,000 towards the public
park now being purchased for Warrington.
There has been a semi-rebellion at the
diamond fields at the Cape, and tents have
been burned. The local authorities called out
special constables and great disorder existed
for some time, during which Lynch law was
paramount. There appears to have existed a
design amongst the worst class of diggers to
harass the natives and some of the lattcr have
been brutally assaulted. The Governor pros
weds to the fields shortly, where he i
anxiously expected. The finds at the gold-
fields are reported to be considerable.

. Charles Harvey, u young convict, employed
on the Chatham Dockyard Extension Works,
was engaged on Tuesday afternoon with a
number of conviets in. stacking bricks, and
suddenly disappeared. A great many guards
and warders watch over the convicts on St.
Mary's Islands-, and bow Harvey managed. to
escape is a puzzule. It is. said that some of
his gang saw him changing his clothes, but
they gave no alarm to the warders, • Harvey is
twenty-two years of age. This was
,his second
term of penal servitude.. He is reputed one of
the cleverest burglars of the day. His last
sentence was twelve years. _

Earl Granville is now the Minister in
attendance upon her Majesty at Balmoral.
One of the Burmese .Ambassadoia, anxious
to introduee the pottery manufaeture into his
native country, is now on a visit to Hanley
with that object in view.
. Barnet. Fair opened on Wednesday, and,
as usual, there was a large attendance of
dealers, not only from all parts of England,
but also from France; Germany, and Holland.
The general show of horses is described as
having been much below the average in
quality.
The directors of the North British Railway,
in their half-yearly report, call attention to
the increased cost of coal and iron, and also to
the general advance in wages. An augmenta-
tion of the rates for the conveyance of
merchandise and mineral traffic will therefore
come into operation in the beginning of next
month.

On Wechiesday the coal merchants of Leeds
made an advance of 53. 10d. per ton in the
price of coal, which is now more than double
the price at which it stood twelve moinths ago.

• Serious defalcations have been discovered in
connection with the Rochdale Pioneers' Co-
operative Society. .The books of the late
treasurer, who died a few days ago, on being
overhauled on Monday evening, revealed a
deficiency amounting nearly to £4OO, and the
cashierhas disappeared, carrying with him the
keys of
•the safe, which was supposed to
contain about .t 212.

In anticipation of the visit of the Prince of
Wales to BaliBbury, the most hearty and
energetic measures have be taken tor the
decoration of that city, The subscriptions for
the adornment of the place already amount to
£BOO, and fresh names are daily being added
to tho list.

For some time past there have violent dis-
putes between the trawlers in Galway Bay and
the Claddagh fishermen, the latter alleging
that the trawlers were encroaching on pro-
hibited ground. On the other band the
trawlers have sworn information against the
Claddagh men, stating—that their lives had
been threatened, and that last week an
attempt was made to burn one of their vessels.
A magisterial investigation has commenced,

THE NATIONAL DEBT.
To the Editor of the BEE-IlIvE.

Srn,—Mr. Rigby Wason hopes Lord Derby
will grant a Committee of the Houses
of Parliament to inquire into the expediency
of paying off the National Debt. I hope his
lordship will do nothing of the kind. What
that is now can be said on tile subject?
The debt can only be paid in two ways—
increased taxation or by the issue of an incon-
vertible currency; both these methods arc in
use in the 'United States.

The objection to the first is that you raise
money at 100 per cent, interest to pay off a
debt floated at 3 pen cent.—that is to say, the
two millions Mr. Gladstone applies annually
towards paying of the debt would supply the
place of the tea duty. The tea duty is 6d.. per
pound; and were it taken off, tea would fall
in price is. per pound, so that this import costs
100 per cent. to collect.
The extent to which an inconvertible
currency can be naturally floated depends on
the extent to which it will naturally supersede
gold. Directly gold is at a premium (say
above £4 per ounce), the evils of the American
greenback system willcome into play. The man
who bargAins for £1 per weak wages, finds his
pound of paper will only fetch 10s., 18s., 17s,
and so on as the premium on sold rises, so
that, as in America, there will be two 'prices
for everything, the one in paper, and the other
in gold.
The consequence of this is that the money
dealer makes his bargains in gold, and pays
in paper; the poor man, as a matter of course,
goes to the wall.
Mankind having been used from the earliest
times to measure the value of everything by
gold, will still continue to do so, and the
moment a paper pound will not buy a gold
pound, 'the value of the paper pound will
sink; in other words there will he a premium
on gold.
Experience has fixed the Average of paper
circulation in the three kingdoms at about 40
millions, and no doubt a saving to the extent
of 3 per cent. thereon, or £1,200,000 per
annum might be " effected.-4 am sir, your
obedient servant,

G. W. FIELD.

THE JOINERS AND THE MASONS.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Sin,—Having had something to do with the
recent agitation and settlement in the build-
ing trades, perhaps you will allow 1116 to say
a few words in answer to your correspondent,
Mr. A. Scott, whose letter is full of misstate-
ments, and evidently an intentional perversion
of the truth. Mr. Scott says the difference
between the masons and join4rs is one of
principle, and may it ever remain so, if the
false slander and abuse contained in the
letter referred is a sample of the principles held
by those at the Brown Bear.
Ignorance of facts may sometimes be
advanced as an excuse for misstatements; such
cannot be Mr. Scott's excuse, because he has
taken an active part in this question, conse-
quently must have known at the time he was
writing his letter that he was penning the
reverse of the truth. Mr. Scott, in the first
place, accuses us of being traitors; such an
accusation emanating from • such a quarter
savours somewhat of the ludicrous, and the
person making it must 'be possessed of a
tolerable amount of impudence, when we
consider who the parties actually were that
expressed such an anxious desire to have an
amalgamated committee of the trade, and
having gratified that desire set about opposing
every action of that committee in a most
systematic manner; and then, at the last
moment, withdrew their delegates, and sent
their own deputation about an hour before the
remainder of the amalgamated committee's
deputation, when that interview was brought
about through the instrumentality of Mr.
Shipton the secretary of the amalgamated
committee, whose action evidently was too
independent to please the Brown Bear com-
mittee, who evidently anticipated having a
committee to receive instructions from the
Brown Bear; but as soon as Mr. Scott and his
friends found that their offspring had suffi-
cient vitality to conduct its own affairs, they
at once threw it over and declared "that it
was beneath consideration."

Mr.. Scott also says "it was generally
understood between the two trades that there
was a mutual agreement between them." A
more barefaced falsehood was never penned,
because, sir, the first time a deputation from
the carpenters attended one of our meetings at
Wilcox's rooms, they sent in a . note to the
chairman requesting to be admitted, which
note the chairman read to the meeting, when
,a general cry arose of no amalgamation, but
on the advice of the chairman they were ad-
mitted, and after one of the deputation had
addressed the meeting, I was requested by
the chairman to explain to the deputation the
feeling of the meeting which had just been ex-
pressed in reference to amalgamation, and the
joiners have had nO cause to think the decision
of that meeting altered in any respect; so
much for the understanding alluded to by Mr.
Scott.

Mr. Scott not states "at any time they,
the carpenters, agreed to appoint a deputation
it was always known to the masons, if they
did not get it officially, they got it senit-
officially through the press," That statement
certainly is true in the abstract, but it is truth
so worded that it is calculated to convey a
very erroneous impression. If Mr. Scott had.
simply said whatever information the masons
obtained of our proceedings was always ob-
tained through the press, be would have
stated the same truth in language that could
not be misconstrued.

Your correspondent also states that ", the
masons held a secret meeting of the officials of
their trade society, and agreed to appoint a
deputation with full power to settle the dis-
pute concerning their trade, and this was
done without the sanction of the general body
of their own trade." Now, Sir, Mr. Scott
either knows nothing at all about the case, or
he is guilty of writing a deliberate lie to serve
his own purpose. In either case his despicable
conduct is deserving the severest censure of
all honourable men. The fact is, the meeting
appointing the deputation was publicly an-
nounced to members in the usual form, the
only reservation was the admission only of
members in benefit, and the production of
their cards at the door, and instead of its
being only a few officials, the room was
crowded to excess by members.
Again, Mr. Scott states that our action was
the means of dragging the joiners into a long
struggle, and asserts his convietion that it
would have been settled, five weeks ego if it

' SEPT. 7,. 1872-i

had not been for the action of Mr. Broadhurst
and his colleagues. I contend the action of
Mr. Broadhurst and those that acted with
him was calculated to have the reverse effe,ct,
because Mr. Sinclair congratulated the meet-
ing of delegates at the Brown Bear of having
got rid of us as a source of weakness. Mr.
Sadler again asserted the action taken by us
had considerably "strengthened their position,
and would materiully increase the support'
rendered to them. Again, Sir, ;Mr. Scott evi-
dently does not choose to remember that the
terms we accepted were offered to them, which
terms are a considerable deal better than those
they have accepted, notwithstanding the
assertion of some of the daily papers to thea.
contrary. Because, Sir, the primary object 01
the late agitation was the reduction of Ole
hours of labour, and I suppose even Mr. Scott
will admit we have obtained a greater redotion of the hours than the carpenters,
and one of the main arguments in fa-
vour of that reduction was the necessity of
finding employment for the surplus labour,
and as there is always more surplus labour lU
the market in winter than any other -portion
of the year, the consequent result is a necessity
for a greater reduction of hours in the winter
months—a reduction that we have made com-
plete, but which the joiners have failed in
doing. Also we have established the twelve
o'clock on Saturday all the year round, a honn
that the building trades have struggled
for in vain previously, and that the other
trades have only partially established
in the winter months, but they, "the oar-
penters," were determined above all things t°
abolish overtime and piece-work. The latter
has been entirely iguored in
.their arrange-
ments, and the former has had but a very
sorry death blow dealt to it. Doee any sane
man for one moment suppose that.the pay-
ment of an extra penny per hour will deter the
employers from resorting to that cursed
system that keeps the employed at the mercy
of the employers,
Even supposing the extra penny a safe-
guard against overtime, they have taken
good care to leave a broad road open for any
amount of overtime to be worked at the
ordinary price, be inserting the clause "that
anyone asking 6) work overtime is to get
nothing extra. So that the abolition of over-
time is a sham and a delusion.—l am, Sir,
yours truly,
FF. NEPBIT.
Chairman of Masons' London Lodges
Committee.
